parsed.narrative.subject: naval ship losses
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist rises angry with his boy for lying in bed and forgetting his lute, then works at his office and dines. In the evening at Gresham College he finds great pleasure in hearing Commissioner Pett and Lord Brunker discourse on Mr. Castle's ship draft. Late that night, a letter from Plymouth reports two of the fleet's ships lost aground and others nearly lost, with a Dutch fleet heading there, which he calls most sad news. Returning home, he is much troubled to find his canary bird, kept three or four years, dead.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mr. Povy's folly
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys went to Lord Ashley's by appointment and watched Povy confound himself with many words and no understanding, which left the committee business unsettled. The group broke up dissatisfied and referred the matter to a later meeting. He noted the awkwardness of sitting with his hat on while Mr. Sherwin stood bare, and said he thanked God he was never the better man for it. Dinner with a brace of pheasants and talk of Povy's folly left him merry, and the day ended with late hours at the office.

He notes that his cousin Percivall Angier was buried today without him present, and that he learned yesterday of the death of Dr. Tom Pepys.

He is too sleepy to keep his eyes open and must break off the entry early. He notes the burial of his cousin Percivall Angier, which he could not attend, and the news of Dr. Tom Pepys's death, for which he is but little sorry.

parsed.narrative.subject: Dr. Tom Pepys's death
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys could not walk the streets because of a great thaw, so he took a coach to Mr. Povy's and then to Exeter House, where the Lords' answer was discussed. He was at the office through the afternoon and evening. He reports a great deal of pain, which he attributes to the change of weather, and is so sleepy he can hardly keep his eyes open. He notes that his cousin Percivall Angier was buried the day of writing, and that he learned the day before of Dr. Tom Pepys's death, for which he is little sorry.
parsed.emotion.bodily_sensation: a great deal of pain; so sleepy I cannot hold open my eyes

parsed.narrative.subject: Jane Welsh
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys was called on by Jane Welsh, Mr. Jervas's maid, who had left her master and was resolved to keep to her sweetheart, Harbing. He tried in a word or two to dissuade her, then sent her away, followed her out, and walked and talked with her for an hour or two. She refused to be counselled to stay out her time with her master, saying it was her fortune to have this man. He ended the episode by landing her back at the Three Cranes and went on to his other business that day.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys is vexed at being given uncertain business to handle, including the Tangier ships. His wife summons him home to complain that Jane must be dismissed. He hears both sides, finds his wife much at fault for her fondness for Tom, and resolves to cure it, though the quarrel brings many high words. To ease his mind he makes himself debtor to Mr. Povy for money he had gained, and he accepts some future loss as the price of a quiet mind. He gives thanks for his fortune of L1257 and works on his accounts until nearly two in the morning.
parsed.narrative.meaning: A quiet mind and to be sure of my owne is worth all.

parsed.narrative.summary: At Westminster and then at the office he is cruelly vexed at being given businesses about getting ships for Tangier. After dinner at the Crowne he returns to the office, where his wife summons him to report how Jane behaves and that Jane must be dismissed. He hears both sides, finds his wife much in fault over her fondness for Tom, and resolves to cure it despite many high words between them. He then makes himself debtor to Mr. Povy for money he got with joy the previous month, to be rid of the worry, and says a quiet mind is worth all. He ends by praising the Lord for what he has and staying up late over his accounts.

parsed.narrative.subject: Povy's accounts
parsed.narrative.summary: At a Committee of Tangier, Lord Ashly, vexed with Povy's accounts, proposed that Povy remain Treasurer until his accounts were settled. The writer, unprepared to answer his arguments, put off the discussion and believed he had set matters right, but it troubled him all day and night. Later, at White Hall, he gave the Lord Treasurer and others an account of the Navy's charge and want of money, and their only response was to ask what should be done. He went home vexed, then spent the evening merrily with the women at Lady Batten's and at his own supper.

Later he hears the fleet news: first reports of Teddiman's wounds are reversed, and he is glad the Royal Katherine is safe.

Pepys was unprepared for the arguments and brought the matter back by putting off the discussion, but it troubled him through the rest of the day and night. Later, after the Council rose, he gave the Lord Treasurer and others a long account of the Navy's charges and lack of money. The reply that nothing could be done left him vexed. He then went to Lady Batten's, where merry company lifted the mood, though he was still vexed as he joined supper and went home to bed.
parsed.narrative.meaning: It is one of the saddest things that nothing was minded at such a time, and things were left to go on as they could.

parsed.narrative.subject: Tangier business
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys rose early and went to Mr. Povy, wanting to end his trouble of mind over the Tangier business and whether Povy would accept the treasurership again. Povy said he would not, which satisfied Pepys for the moment. Creed then cast doubt on this, citing the auditors' reasons, and gave advice on what to do. Pepys then arranged an order for Povy's remaining accounts to be paid to him, which he hoped would stop the matter being fastened on him. Later that day, news of the fleets' engagement was reported, but before night he heard the contrary: all were well and the Royall Katherine was likely to prove a good ship, which he was heartily glad of.

parsed.narrative.subject: Tangier business
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys goes to Povy wanting to end his worry over the Tangier business and whether Povy will take back the treasurer post. Povy says he would not, which satisfies Pepys for the moment. After talking with Creed, Pepys doubts this, because the auditors' reasons seem plain and hard to withstand. He then secures an order from Lord Barkeley and the Commissioners for Povy's remaining accounts to be paid to him, which he hopes will stop the work being fastened on him. Later that day, news that the fleets were engaged and that Captain Teddiman was wounded is replaced by word that all were well and the Royall Katherine has joined the fleet, which pleases him.

parsed.narrative.subject: the King's recognition
parsed.narrative.summary: At the Duke of Albemarle's Pepys hears news of captured Dutch privateers and the Smyrna fleet sighted off Scotland, and the King orders a fleet northward. At White Hall the King approaches him, calls him by name and discusses the ships in the River. Pepys records that this is the first time he knew the King knew him personally, so he must now expect to be questioned and be ready with good answers. He then dines, attends a play, and returns home to work at his office.

parsed.narrative.subject: Tangier treasurership
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys went early to Mr. Povy, wishing to end his trouble of mind over the Tangier business, and offered him back the treasurership on his own terms. Povy refused, and Pepys was briefly satisfied. Speaking with Creed later raised doubt that Povy would have to be reinstated, and Pepys then secured an order for Povy's payment of accounts to him, which he hoped would stop the blame falling on him. The next morning he heard news of a fleet engagement and the loss of Captain Teddiman's legs, but before night the news was contrary: all were well and the Royal Katherine had joined the fleet.

parsed.narrative.subject: Tangier commission
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys walked with Sir Philip Warwicke for an hour in the Park, which he describes as a great delight, discussing Sir G. Carteret's accounts. At noon he went by water with his wife and Mr. Moore to Chelsea for his Privy Seal for Tangier, but the Lord Privy Seal was out, so they had to return without landing. After Sir Philip took him to the Lord Treasurer, who signed his commission and the docquet, he went again to Whitehall, failed to find the Lord, and went home. He ended the day working late at his office before supper and bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Tangier Privy Seal
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys walked for an hour with Sir Philip Warwicke in the Park, describing it as a great delight, and discussed Sir G. Carteret's accounts. At noon he went by water with his wife and Mr. Moore to Chelsea for his Privy Seal for Tangier, but the Lord Privy Seal had gone out, so they had to return without leaving the boat. Warwicke then took him to the Lord Treasurer, who signed his Tangier-Treasurer commission and the docquet for the monies. Pepys then returned to Whitehall, failed to find the Lord, and went home, and the day ended with late office work, supper and bed.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys went to Chelsea expecting trouble over his Tangier Privy Seal, but Lord Privy Seal passed it at first reading without a conversation and was civil to him. He returned to London very joyful and told Povy, then moved through the Exchange, Trinity House and Gresham College. There Povy gave him 'most exceeding discouragements' about getting money, which left him in 'a cruel melancholy'. He ended the day hoping that tomorrow would show something, with his head aching, and went to bed around 10 or 11.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mr. Andrews loan
parsed.narrative.summary: The subject spends the morning at the office and dines at noon with Mr. Povy, whose boldness with Mercer makes both the subject and Mercer blush. After dinner Creed and then Andrews arrive, and Andrews's want of money becomes the main topic. Trusting Creed's judgement, the subject resolves to spare Andrews 4 or L500 from funds held on the security of some tallies. He says this went against his heart to begin, but once Creed agrees to join him they resolve to assist Andrews. That evening he hears that the first play has been staged in the White Hall noon-hall, and he had a great mind to see it but could not go.

parsed.narrative.summary: On Lord's Day, the 23rd, the diarist attends Whitehall Chapel with his wife and hears the young Stillingfleet preach, which he calls the plainest, most honest and most substantial sermon he has ever heard. An argument with Taylor over a Corant vexes the diarist, but the company parts friends and he and Creed laugh at Taylor afterward.

parsed.narrative.summary: In the morning Pepys worked at the office, then obtained the Lord Treasurer's signature on a warrant and ran errands on his way home. He was troubled to hear that Sir W. Batten and Sir J. Minnes noticed his absence from the office, and more troubled that he had neglected to write to Mr. Coventry, committing blots in the letter he wrote late that night. On the Lord's day he made up his monthly accounts alone and found, with great joy, that he had gained over L100 that month and was worth above L1400, the greatest sum he had yet held. He closed the month in great content about his estate, but in much trouble about the pains and expected difficulties of the Tangier business.

parsed.narrative.subject: funeral of Sir Thomas Viner
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist put on a new silk camelott suit, which he says was the best he had ever worn, and went with Creed to Goldsmiths' Hall for the burial of Sir Thomas Viner. The halls were too crowded, so he went out to Pater Noster Row to choose silk for a plain suit. In the afternoon and evening he went by coach to Westminster Hall and Tothill Fields, and he describes his pleasure in the encounter without further detail. He returned home to write letters and ended the day hearing news that the fleet was in sight of the Dutch ships.

parsed.narrative.subject: fleet news
parsed.narrative.summary: The writer's wife and mother went by boat to Gravesend in the morning, and he worked at the office on Sir G. Carteret's accounts. He dined with colleagues at the Dolphin Tavern and was very merry. On a very hot day he drank whey at the New Exchange and then walked with great pleasure at Spring Garden, though he was uneasy about the fleet and Lord Sandwich, with no news and unfounded reports of his death. He waited at Whitehall for news, found none, and walked in his garden until midnight awaiting his wife, then went to bed. That day in Drury Lane he saw houses marked with a red cross, which he called a sad sight and the first of its kind he remembered, so he bought tobacco to smell and chew.

parsed.narrative.summary: The writer spent the day on office business and dined with colleagues, describing merriment at the Dolphin Tavern. In the afternoon's extreme heat he sought whey and then walked at Spring Garden with great pleasure, though his mind was uneasy about the fleet and Lord Sandwich, with no news and unfounded rumours of Sandwich's death. parsed.narrative.subject: Lord Sandwich's honour
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist lay long in bed with a head aching from too many thoughts. He was troubled that he had heard nothing of Lord Sandwich's conduct, until Mr. Moore told him the King had said Sandwich had done nobly and worthily, which eased him. Prompted by joy at the recent victory over the Dutch, he bought a coloured silk suit after long resolving to wear only black. In the evening guests came to a supper held in place of his stone-feast, and they were very merry before parting, and he went to bed glad the day was over.

parsed.narrative.subject: news of the fleet
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spent the hot day at the office and dining with colleagues, and was merry. Later he walked at Spring Garden with great pleasure, though uneasy about the fleet and Lord Sandwich, with no news and only unfounded rumours of Sandwich's death. He came home weary and waited in vain for his wife, walking in the garden until midnight, when lightning began. Earlier in Drury Lane he saw houses marked with red crosses, a sad sight, and bought roll-tobacco to smell, which took away his apprehension.

parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist lay in bed with an aching head from too many thoughts and was troubled about Lord Sandwich's standing. Mr. Moore eased that worry by reporting the King's praise of Sandwich. Glad of the recent news of victory over the Dutch, he bought a coloured silk suit, which he had not done before. That evening friends came to supper, and the diarist records being very merry and liking Mr. Honiwood's conversation more. He ended the day glad that the evening was over.

parsed.narrative.subject: Duke of Yorke's return
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys went to the office, then to White Hall, where the court was full of the Duke of York and his courtiers returned from sea. After a long wait he met Mr. Coventry, which rejoiced his heart, and they discussed naval business in the Matted Gallery. He recorded reports of captains' conduct, including Holmes's resignation and Grovel's cowardice at Lowestoft. He then noted the Dutch claim of victory and Coventry's estimate of the losses, and went home to supper.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mr. Coventry
parsed.narrative.summary: The writer goes to White Hall, where the court is full of the Duke of York and his returned courtiers. After a long wait he sees Mr. Coventry, which rejoices his very heart. parsed.narrative.subject: shut-up plague house
parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist went to Whitehall and the Committee of Tangier, where a promised sum was judged short but acceptable if his own debts could be paid. He dined and talked business with associates, and his wife's brother came asking for a living, which he promised to consider. Later he went by water to Woolwich and walked back, weighing a summer stay there for his wife. On the way home he saw a house shut up in the open street, which he called a sad sight, as the plague grew.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys walked to Greenwich with Captains who criticized Captain Teddiman's handling of the Bergen business. parsed.narrative.subject: Swakely visit
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys rises early, fearful of an ague, and goes by water to the Tower, where he reads the weekly bill and finds 8,252 dead, 6,878 of them from plague, which he calls a most dreadful number. He then travels to Brainford and on to Sir R. Viner's pleasant house at Swakely, where he is shown the house and grounds with great respect. He dines, hears songs in the long gallery with great delight, and completes his business to his content. He returns by water to Woolwich, arriving about one in the morning.

parsed.narrative.subject: boy Jacke's illness
parsed.narrative.summary: At Greenwich, around 4 or 5 in the morning, the narrator and Captain Cocke heard that Lord Bruncker's boy Jacke had gone to bed sick, complaining mostly of his head. Both were troubled, and the narrator concealed his own fear, then went to bed and slept until 10. Captain Cocke woke him to say the boy was well again, and the narrator heard this with great joy. The day that followed included dinner, office work, and an evening supper marked by a family feud and general disorder.

parsed.narrative.subject: Cocke's sick boy
parsed.narrative.summary: At Greenwich, the narrator and Captain Cocke heard that Cocke's boy Jacke had gone to bed sick, complaining mostly of his head, and both were much troubled. The narrator did not want to show too much fear, slept, and was woken by Cocke with news that the boy was well again. He reports great joy at this news. Later that evening, the supper at Sir J. Minnes's ended in disorder and a feud after the company left without taking leave, and the narrator found a lodging arranged by W. Hewer, which he describes as a very fine room.

parsed.narrative.summary: Captain Cocke reported that his boy was now well, which brought relief in the morning. At the Duke of Albemarle's, the Duke showed the week's plague figures, which had risen by about 600 against hopes from the cold season and exceeded the biggest bill yet. parsed.narrative.subject: night boat journey
parsed.narrative.summary: The writer and his party reached the fleet and dealt with Sir Roger Cuttance and others, then went in haste to Chatham by wherry as darkness fell. Their simple waterman did not know the way, so they went back and forth in the dark, which vexed them greatly. They took on a fisher boy who was odd and would not answer aloud, but he carried them safely with a mistake or two. They were surprised by the sea-water glowing like fire at each stroke of the oar, and at the Crowne Inn in Rochester they made merry with the boy before going to bed in their clothes.
parsed.narrative.meaning: Glad to have escaped signing the undertaking for the whole sum.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys is told that Captain Cocke's boy is now well, which comforts him. He then learns from the Duke of Albemarle that plague deaths rose by about 600 that week, against all hopes, and calls this very grievous to them all. He stops a plan to add merchants to a ship inspection, which he thinks would have harmed the King, though he admits some envy at others taking profitable business. After dinner with Lord Bruncker's household he writes letters for a journey the next day and ends the day very weary.

parsed.narrative.subject: night boat journey
parsed.narrative.summary: After a day of business at Chatham, the narrator and companions set off by boat in haste as the calm water and growing darkness slowed them. They lost their way, which vexed them greatly, and they took on a fisher boy who would not answer aloud but did carry them safely with a mistake or two. parsed.narrative.subject: night boat journey
parsed.narrative.summary: After a long discussion aboard the Prince, a bargain for silks, cinnamon, nutmeg and indigo was agreed. The narrator nearly signed an undertaking for the whole sum but escaped it by chance, and later judged himself glad of it. Setting out by wherry toward Chatham after dark, the party was confused by a waterman who did not know the way and by an unhelpful fisher boy, which vexed them. They reached the Crown Inn at Rochester, where they supped merrily with the boy and went to bed in their clothes.

parsed.narrative.summary: After a dinner that left him merry, he returned to Woolwich and found his wife unwell. She told him in private of her falling out with her maids, especially Mary, who had threatened to say something that would stop her mouth. parsed.narrative.summary: After a merry, pleasing dinner with company, Pepys returned home to Woolwich and found his wife upset over a falling out with her maids, especially Mary. He felt great trouble and, being jealous, grew out of temper and left in a passion, intending to return to his ship. On reflection he decided it was better to sleep in a good bed and be with his wife, and resolved to salve the business rather than stir it. He went to sleep content, reckoning that the last three months had brought him the greatest joy, health and profit of his life, despite the plague.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mrs. Daniel and Sarah
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys walked to Redriffe and then to London, where he was briefly displeased by his wife's attention to her brother and sister. He spent the day on business, settled his money matters to his satisfaction, and dined merrily at the Pope's Head, though he privately mocked Dr. Hinton's manner. That evening Mr. Pierce reported that W. Howe had charged him with using Lord Bruncker's name, and this vexed Pepys that his name was brought into question. He ended the night at cards with Mrs. Tooker, having great pleasure with his little girl.

He is pleased with his cleared money matters and his contentment in the day's work. He spies Mrs. Daniel and Sarah in Cornhill, dogs them, passes them shyly, and searches for them without success. At dinner with Sir W. Warren and others he is merry and amused by Dr. Hinton's manner, and later returns by water to Greenwich, frightened by the ice. At his lodgings, Mr. Pierce reports that W. Howe has used Lord Bruncker's name out of envy, which vexes Pepys that his own name is questioned. He ends the evening at cards with Mrs. Tooker, having great pleasure with her.
parsed.context.event: day of business, dinner and cards

parsed.narrative.summary: At noon he dined with colleagues at Captain Cocke's and was merry despite being frost-bitten. The entry closes with a visit from Mrs. Burrows, a former acquaintance, whom he kissed.

parsed.narrative.subject: accounts and money
parsed.narrative.summary: On a fine frosty morning he walked to Lambeth and met colleagues at the Duke of Albemarle's, then took a coach to the Exchange, where he greeted his seamstress and dined with Sir Ellis Layton and others. In the evening, after supper with Mrs. Penington at the King's Head, he asked her to undress for a sketch and walked outside while she did, then went home to be spoken with by Mrs. Daniel about her husband. He was pleased with recent money gains, but two things troubled him: the sickness rising above 80 that week and an account so tangled over two months that he cannot reconcile it as he once did at home.

parsed.narrative.subject: Navy business and money dealings
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys walked to Lambeth on a fine frosty morning and spent an hour on Navy business at the Duke of Albemarle's. At the Exchange he visited his seamstress and paid for stockings, then handled money at Lombard Street. In the evening, after supper with Mrs. Penington, he went walking in the cold dark while she undressed, and was pleased about his money this month. He then said two things troubled him: the sickness had risen above 80 that week, and his accounts for two months were too complex for him to reconcile.

parsed.narrative.subject: settling accounts
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends the morning on new instructions for signing and paying bills, and recommends Poynter as a clerk to the Controller, which he accepts. At noon Mr. Hill and Mr. Houbland arrive, and Pepys is compelled to dine with them at the Beare, where the company is merry. Mr. Andrews is brought to accept tallies for Tangier victualling orders, clearing L210 that Pepys counts as a welcome addition to his profits. Pepys says his unfinished accounts burden his mind, and he resolves to settle nothing else until they are done; after an evening watching Lord Bruncker remake a watch, he records his journal to ease his mind.

parsed.context.place: navy office, the Beare, Lord Bruncker's lodging

parsed.narrative.subject: tallies payment
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends the day on official business at the Navy Office, including reading new instructions and recommending a clerk to the Controller. At noon, after guests arrive, he is pulled away from Lord Bruncker's company to dine at the Beare, where he finds the company merry and is glad to see them. Mr. Andrews is brought to accept tallies for orders to pay for Tangier victuals, which clears L210 to Pepys, a welcome addition to his profits. He notes that the unfinished accounts burden his mind, and he resolves to settle nothing until they are done.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mrs. Daniel's supper
parsed.narrative.summary: At noon the diarist dined with Captain Cocke and others, merry despite being frost-bitten. Going home that evening, his head was full of business and trouble over letting his accounts go so far, and he had sworn an oath against drinking wine until they were passed. At home, the boy reported that his sister Daniel had prepared a supper of little birds for him, and he kept her company after supper and enjoyed her kisses. The same day, Mrs. Burrows, a former acquaintance, also came to visit, and he had a kiss or two from her.

parsed.narrative.subject: unfinished accounts
parsed.narrative.summary: The writer rises early and works with colleagues on new instructions for signing and paying bills. He recommends Poynter as a clerk to the Controller, which relieves him of a man he feared would not suit his own needs. At noon Mr. Hill and Mr. Houbland arrive, and he leaves his lord's dinner to dine with them at the Beare, which he enjoys. Later, Mr. Andrews agrees to take tallys for payments, giving him L210, and he says his accounts burden his mind until he has finished them. In the evening he watches Lord Bruncker open and reassemble a watch and is pleased, then is briefly vexed by Madam Williams's snappish reply before he settles his journal and goes to bed.
parsed.emotion.meta: resolved to finish accounts before other engagements
parsed.context.event: office work, dinner and evening visit
parsed.context.place: Beare tavern and Lord Bruncker's house

parsed.narrative.subject: bills and accounts
parsed.narrative.summary: In the morning, the writer and colleagues considered new instructions on signing and paying bills, and he recommended Poynter to the Controller as a clerk. At noon Mr. Hill and Mr. Houbland arrived, and he left his lord's dinner to dine with them at the Beare, finding their company merry. After a payment matter with Mr. Andrews cleared L210, he noted his profits but said his unfinished accounts burdened his mind. That evening, at Lord Bruncker's, he watched the watch being opened and remade, which pleased and satisfied him, and he was vexed by Madam Williams's snappish answer to his jest.
parsed.context.event: office work and Christmas social gathering
